title: D-002: Phase-Gated Implementation
body:
# D-002: Phase-Gated Implementation

**Date:** 2026-03-28
**Status:** Active

## Decision

Build in six phases, each with explicit completion gates. Phase 1 = foundation and doctrine. No phase implements logic before its infrastructure dependencies are established in prior phases.

## Why

Building MCP servers, command implementations, and agent behaviors all at once guarantees that early decisions about one component contaminate others before the design is stable. Phasing ensures each layer is solid before the next is built on it.

The specific phase ordering reflects the dependency structure of the framework:
- Phase 1 (Foundation): Establishes the architecture contract — directory structure, schema definitions, doctrine files, stub command and agent specs. Nothing is implemented, but everything is specified.
- Phase 2 (Knowledge Infrastructure): Implements guide-server and cache-server. Knowledge retrieval and run state management must exist before agents can consume them.
- Phase 3 (Writing Pipeline): Implements the commands and agents that produce document content. These require the schemas from Phase 1 and the infrastructure from Phase 2.
- Phase 4 (QA): Implements the seven QA perspectives. QA must follow writing pipeline implementation because QA evaluates outputs that require the pipeline to produce.
- Phase 5 (Artifacts): Implements artifact generation and export. Artifact generation follows QA because only QA-approved outputs are exported.
- Phase 6 (Portability): Implements sync, export-pack, import-pack, and install-framework. Portability is built last because you cannot make a system portable until you understand what it is.

## Alternatives Considered

**Build everything in one pass.** Rejected: produces unmaintainable scope and forces premature implementation decisions. The most common failure mode of this approach is that early implementation choices lock in architectural decisions that should remain open until the design stabilizes.

## Consequences

Phase 1 files are stubs. Phase 2 implements guide-server and cache-server. Phase 3 adds the writing pipeline. This means Phase 1 is not "working" in the functional sense — it is the architecture contract that all subsequent phases implement against. Agents encountering Phase 1 stubs should not attempt to execute them — they should classify missing implementations as B5 (failed toolchain) blockers until the relevant phase is complete.
